name: funtrace
baseline: LLVM XRay flight recorder logging and uftrace (call tracers)
workload: Per-call overhead of function entry/return tracing in a microbenchmark.
claimed_speedup: <10 ns per instrumented call or return; 6x faster than XRay flight recorder logging, 15-18x faster than XRay basic logging, 4.5x faster than uftrace
compiler_and_flags: gcc/clang with -finstrument-functions, -pg -mfentry or -fxray-instrument (benchmark flags not stated on README)
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only; tracing profiler (must choose what to trace, higher overhead than sampling perf); needs compiler instrumentation; tail call and exception artifacts.
caveats: Author's own microbenchmark, hardware and exact flags not stated on README; baselines are XRay and uftrace, not perf/gprof/Valgrind. Author notes uftrace targets a different workflow.
found_via: Package registries: WebSearch 'uftrace magic-trace hawktracer perfetto overhead compared gprof Valgrind' surfaced the repo; README opened

name: aw-backtrace
baseline: libgcc _Unwind_Backtrace and LLVM libunwind (stack unwinders used by profilers)
workload: Microbenchmark of unwind cost per frame on recursive stacks, mostly cache hits (recursion-test.cc).
claimed_speedup: ~9 ns per unwind step vs libgcc ~53-55 ns and LLVM libunwind ~287-292 ns per step; README: libgcc about 5x slower, LLVM libunwind another 5x slower than libgcc
tradeoffs: Linux glibc 2.35+ (_dl_find_object) on x86-64 and aarch64; API not stable, no install story, Bazel build; frame-pointer unwinding is still ~10x faster.
caveats: Benchmark code is public but CPU model is not stated, so not tier A. Microbenchmark is mostly cache hits. Project first released September 2026, very new. Baselines are unwinders, not perf/gprof/Valgrind.
found_via: Package registries: WebSearch 'aw-backtrace OR eh_elf backtrace library without libunwind fast benchmark github'

name: Dr. Memory
workload: Memory error checking (uninitialized reads, heap errors, leaks) on SPEC CPU2006 on Linux, CGO 2011 paper.
claimed_speedup: On average twice as fast as Memcheck, up to four times faster on individual benchmarks; ran 434.zeusmp and 447.dealII that Memcheck could not (from paper abstract as quoted in search results and repo README)
tradeoffs: Built on DynamoRIO; supports Windows, Linux, Mac, Android on x86/ARM; fewer checks than Memcheck in some areas.
caveats: Paper from 2011 (old numbers). The PDF was not opened (blocked); figures come from the repo README and a search snippet of the paper. A GitHub issue reports a benchmark (adamdunkels-ubasic) where Dr. Memory timed out after 2 hours while Memcheck took about 2 minutes, so the win is workload dependent.
found_via: Package registries: WebSearch 'Dr. Memory faster than Valgrind Memcheck slowdown benchmark github DynamoRIO'

name: Palanteer
baseline: spdlog (logging) and NanoLog; profiler instrumentation cost
workload: Runtime cost and compile time of a logging call in the instrumentation library.
claimed_speedup: ~50x faster at runtime than spdlog, only twice slower than NanoLog, 6x faster compiling a log call than spdlog; ~25 ns per event; up to ~5 million events per second recording
license: MIT (instrumentation libraries); AGPL-3.0-or-later (viewer and scripting module)
tradeoffs: Beta state; evolving protocol and storage formats; viewer is AGPL.
caveats: Baseline is a logging library, not perf/gprof/Valgrind; README claims only, benchmark code and hardware not located. Only partial fit to the category.
found_via: Package registries: WebFetch of the repo README after profiler search

name: ClickHouse libunwind stack-trace cache (llvm-project fork)
baseline: LLVM libunwind before the change (stack unwinder used by ClickHouse's sampling profiler)
workload: benchmark_stack_trace microbenchmark: repeated stacks, exceptions, cache-missing call sites and profiler-style samples from a signal handler.
claimed_speedup: Stack trace capture (45 frames, depth 64) 8594 to 1351 ns (6.36x x86-64), 22480 to 3093 ns (7.27x AArch64); exception throw/catch depth 16 17418 to 3661 ns (4.76x), 41174 to 7091 ns (5.81x AArch64)
license: Apache-2.0 (LLVM exception) for the fork; ClickHouse Apache-2.0
tradeoffs: Change lives in ClickHouse's vendored fork of llvm-project (contrib/llvm-project); not a standalone library.
caveats: Before/after of the project's own change, not a public shootout; flags not stated; fork repo itself was not opened, so repo_url points at the PR host repo. Baseline is old libunwind, not perf/gprof/Valgrind.
found_via: Package registries: WebSearch 'stack unwinding sampling profiler library faster than libunwind perf github benchmark'

name: heaptrack
workload: Heap allocation profiling of real applications; only allocation calls are intercepted via LD_PRELOAD, CPU-bound code runs at native speed.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: overhead in time and memory 'significantly lower' than Massif; multi-threaded programs are not serialized
tradeoffs: Massif can also profile stack and page-level allocations, which heaptrack cannot do efficiently; Linux only.
caveats: Qualitative claim only. Repo has a LICENSES folder (SPDX multi-licence, likely LGPL-2.1-or-later and others) but the exact id was not confirmed from the page, so usability is set conservatively to reference; verifier should check. Author blog (milianw.de) blocked.
found_via: Package registries: WebSearch 'heaptrack faster than Valgrind massif overhead heap profiler'
